analysis.one_liner: Exempts noninvasive diagnostic devices from FDA regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote and died in committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal food and drug law so that diagnostic devices which don't pierce, enter, or irradiate the body — things like some lab tests and sensors that press against the skin — would no longer be regulated as medical devices by the FDA. Makers of those tests could sell them without the FDA reviewing whether they are safe and accurate. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Makers of noninvasive diagnostic devices, such as skin-contacting sensors and certain lab tests, gain by skipping FDA review of their products, cutting the time and cost of bringing them to market. Patients might see some new tests reach the market faster, but without any FDA check on whether the tests actually work.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act so that 'non-invasive diagnostic devices' — those that do not penetrate the skin, are not implanted, cause only brief compression or temperature changes, and use no ionizing radiation — are exempted from regulation as devices [S3].
For manufacturers, this removes the FDA review process for this class of diagnostics, lowering the cost and time of bringing products to market [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Patients and their doctors would bear the risk of unvalidated tests: without FDA oversight, an inaccurate or unsafe noninvasive diagnostic could reach the market with no federal check on its claims. A wrong result from a diagnostic test can mean a missed diagnosis or unnecessary treatment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients relying on unreviewed test results

drawbacks.text: The bill removes FDA review entirely for this class of devices rather than streamlining it, so tests with no evidence of accuracy could be marketed as diagnostics [S2][S3].
Patients who receive a wrong result from an unreviewed diagnostic — a false negative on a condition, or a false alarm — would have no assurance the product met any federal standard before sale [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster, cheaper market entry for a narrow category of diagnostic devices; the cost is that the same category loses all federal safety and accuracy oversight. A supporter might argue noninvasive tests carry low physical risk, but a diagnostic's main danger is a wrong answer, which is not addressed by the exemption.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee and never received a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs (R-AZ) introduced the bill on January 9, 2023 [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote is recorded in the action history, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the FDA's authority to review noninvasive diagnostic devices remained intact, so the status quo that patients rely on was preserved; no interest gained ground.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: FDA oversight remained; no one gained ground

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee; it drew no cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and there were no cosponsors, so no party alignment can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would let these companies sell diagnostics without FDA review of safety or accuracy, cutting their regulatory costs while shifting the risk of bad test results to patients. Their gain comes from keeping a review that protects patients off the table.
An exemption carved out for one category would let unreviewed noninvasive tests compete against FDA-cleared diagnostics that bore the cost of review.
